unitTitle: Set Operations (Mengenoperationen), Power Sets (Potenzmengen), and Partitions (Partitionen)
overview: This unit examines relations between sets, core set operations, and their connection to logical connectives (Junktoren). Venn and Karnaugh–Veitch diagrams represent membership cases. For finite sets, cardinality (Mächtigkeit) counts the distinct elements; the power set contains every subset and has exactly 2ᵏ elements when the set has k elements. Families of sets generalize union and intersection to multiple sets, while partitions divide a set into nonempty, pairwise disjoint blocks whose union is the whole set.

entries.short: The universal set Ω specifies which elements belong to the domain under consideration.
entries.explanation: A nonempty universal set Ω is specified for complements and Venn diagrams. The sets M₁ and M₂ under consideration are subsets of Ω. A set's complement depends on this choice: it contains the elements of Ω that are not in the set.
pitfalls: A complement is not uniquely determined unless a universal set has been specified.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: M₁ ⊆ M₂ means that every element of M₁ also belongs to M₂.
entries.explanation: The notation $M_1\subseteq M_2$ allows the two sets to be equal. By contrast, $M_1\nsubseteq M_2$ means that there is at least one element in $M_1$ that is not in $M_2$; equivalently, $M_1\setminus M_2\ne\varnothing$. The sets may still have elements in common.
entries.example: For M₁ = {1, 2} and M₂ = {1, 2, 3}, M₁ ⊆ M₂. For M₃ = {2, 4}, M₃ ⊈ M₂ because 4 is not in M₂.
pitfalls: To establish $M_1\nsubseteq M_2$, one counterexample suffices; not every element of M₁ has to lie outside M₂.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: M₁ is a proper subset of M₂ if M₁ ⊆ M₂ and M₁ ≠ M₂.
entries.explanation: The notation $M_1\subset M_2$ requires every element of $M_1$ to belong to $M_2$ and at least one element of $M_2$ to be absent from $M_1$. Unlike $\subseteq$, this relation excludes equality.
entries.example: {a, b} ⊂ {a, b, c}, since c belongs only to the second set.
pitfalls: Under this symbol convention, the bar in $\subseteq$ allows equality; $\subset$ means proper subset.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: M₁ is a superset of M₂ if M₂ ⊆ M₁.
entries.explanation: The notation $M_1\supseteq M_2$ is read as “M₁ is a superset of M₂.” It is exactly the subset relation with the sets in reverse order. The sets may be equal.
entries.example: For M₁ = {a, b, c} and M₂ = {b}, M₁ ⊇ M₂.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: Two sets are equal if and only if each is a subset of the other.
entries.explanation:
$M_1=M_2\iff (M_1\subseteq M_2\land M_2\subseteq M_1)$ holds. Correspondingly, $M_1
e M_2\iff (M_1
subseteq M_2\lor M_2
subseteq M_1)$ holds. Thus, proving equality requires showing both inclusions.
entries.example: To see that M₁ = {1, 2} and M₂ = {2, 1} are equal, check that both sets contain the same elements.
pitfalls: In general, showing inclusion in only one direction is not enough to establish equality.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: Two sets are disjoint if they have no elements in common.
entries.explanation: M₁ and M₂ are disjoint if and only if $M_1\cap M_2=\varnothing$. Their intersection contains the elements that belong to both sets; for disjoint sets, this intersection is empty.
entries.example: The sets {1, 3} and {2, 4} are disjoint because their intersection is ∅.
pitfalls: Disjointness does not mean that the sets together make up the universal set.
entries.heading: Grundmenge und Beziehungen zwischen Mengen

entries.short: Set operations form new sets from given sets according to their membership conditions.
entries.explanation: The core operations are union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference, and complement relative to a universal set Ω. Whether an element belongs to the result is determined by a condition on its membership in the input sets. These conditions correspond to patterns of logical connectives.
entries.example: An element belongs to the intersection exactly when it belongs to both input sets.
pitfalls: Difference is directional: the result depends on which set is written first.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: The union M₁ ∪ M₂ contains the elements that belong to at least one of the two sets.
entries.explanation: $x\in M_1\cup M_2\iff (x\in M_1\lor x\in M_2)$ holds. The “or” is inclusive: an element that belongs to both sets is also in the union.
pitfalls: An element in the intersection is listed only once in the union.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: The intersection M₁ ∩ M₂ contains exactly the elements that belong to both sets.
entries.explanation: $x\in M_1\cap M_2\iff (x\in M_1\land x\in M_2)$ holds. The intersection describes the elements the sets have in common.
entries.example: For M₁ = {1, 2} and M₂ = {2, 3}, M₁ ∩ M₂ = {2}.
pitfalls: Elements that belong to only one of the two sets are not in the intersection.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: The difference M₁ \ M₂ contains the elements of M₁ that are not in M₂.
entries.explanation: $M_1\setminus M_2=\{x\in M_1\mid x\notin M_2\}$ holds. The order matters: in general, $M_1\setminus M_2$ and $M_2\setminus M_1$ are different.
entries.example: For M₁ = {1, 2, 3} and M₂ = {2, 3, 4}, M₁ \ M₂ = {1}, but M₂ \ M₁ = {4}.
pitfalls: Difference is not symmetric.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: The symmetric difference M₁ △ M₂ contains exactly the elements that belong to one set but not both.
entries.explanation: $M_1\triangle M_2=(M_1\setminus M_2)\cup(M_2\setminus M_1)$ holds. Thus, an element belongs to the symmetric difference if it is in exactly one of the input sets; this corresponds to exclusive or.
entries.example: For M₁ = {1, 2} and M₂ = {2, 3}, M₁ △ M₂ = {1, 3}.
pitfalls: Elements in the intersection are not part of the symmetric difference.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: The complement of M relative to Ω contains the elements of Ω that are not in M.
entries.explanation: One writes $\neg M$ or $\Omega\setminus M$, and $\neg M=\Omega\setminus M$ holds. Thus, only elements of the universal set Ω belong to the complement. The choice of Ω determines the result.
entries.example: For Ω = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} and M = {0, 1, 2}, the complement is {3, 4}.
pitfalls: A complement is relative to the universal set and may differ when a different universal set Ω is chosen.
entries.heading: Mengenoperationen

entries.short: A membership pattern specifies, for each set under consideration, whether an element belongs to it.
entries.explanation: For n sets under consideration, there are $2^n$ possible yes-or-no patterns. For two sets, for example, `10` denotes an element that is in M₁ but not M₂; `00` means it is in neither set, though it may still belong to the universal set Ω. A pattern is only a possibility: in a particular situation, some patterns may not be realized by any element.
entries.example: For M₁ and M₂, `11` denotes an element in their intersection, and `01` denotes an element that belongs only to M₂.
pitfalls: Not every possible pattern has to contain actual elements.
In bit strings encoding subsets, a bit marks whether an element is selected; in membership patterns, it marks whether the element belongs to a set under consideration.
entries.heading: Dieselben Fälle im Venn- und KV-Diagramm

entries.short: A Venn diagram represents sets and their membership regions geometrically within a universal set.
entries.explanation: The universal set Ω is viewed as the outer region, and the sets under consideration are drawn as regions within it. Overlaps show shared membership; regions outside the sets still lie in Ω. This allows the results of set operations to be shown as selected regions.
entries.example: For two overlapping circles, the overlap is the region M₁ ∩ M₂.
pitfalls: A region shown in the diagram may be empty if no element satisfies its corresponding membership pattern.
entries.heading: Venn- und Karnaugh-Veitch-Diagramme

entries.short: A Karnaugh–Veitch diagram (KV diagram) arranges membership cases in the cells of a table.
entries.explanation: Each cell represents a yes-or-no pattern for the sets under consideration. For two sets, the four cells are `00`, `01`, `10`, and `11`; for three, four, and five sets, there are 8, 16, and 32 possible patterns, respectively. A cell and the correspondingly marked region in the Venn diagram represent the same case.
entries.example: In a KV diagram for M₁ and M₂, the cell `10` corresponds to the region M₁ \ M₂.
pitfalls: A cell represents a possible case; it does not have to contain any actual elements.
entries.heading: Venn- und Karnaugh-Veitch-Diagramme

entries.short: The membership conditions of set operations correspond to the truth conditions of logical connectives.
entries.explanation: For a property P(x) over a universal set Ω, the corresponding set is $M_P=\{x\in\Omega\mid P(x)\}$. Negation, conjunction, and inclusive disjunction then correspond to complement, intersection, and union; exclusive disjunction corresponds to symmetric difference. Sets and connectives are different kinds of objects, but the conditions for an element to belong have the same pattern.
entries.example: If P(x) means “x is even” and Q(x) means “x is positive,” the intersection describes the numbers for which both P(x) and Q(x) hold.
pitfalls: Union corresponds to inclusive or; elements in both sets are not excluded.
Symmetric difference corresponds to exclusive or.
entries.heading: Verbindung zur Logik

entries.term: Compact notation for set operations (Kurzschreibweisen der Mengenoperationen)
entries.short: Operation symbols compactly express membership conditions that can be described by forming sets from a fixed set.
entries.explanation: Intersection, difference, and complement can be described using separation from a fixed set. Symmetric difference can also be expressed as the union of the two one-sided differences. These notations make recurring conditions concise and easy to read.
entries.example: The condition “x belongs to M₁ and not to M₂” is written as M₁ \ M₂.
entries.heading: Verbindung zur Logik

entries.short: A set is finite if it can be listed using finitely many objects.
entries.explanation: A set M is finite if there exist $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and objects $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ such that $M=\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}$ holds. For k = 0, the list is empty and denotes the empty set. A set that is not finite is called infinite.
entries.example: The set {a, b} is finite because it can be listed using two objects.
pitfalls: Repeated items in a list do not create additional elements.
entries.heading: Endliche Mengen und Mächtigkeit

entries.short: The cardinality of a finite set counts its distinct elements.
entries.explanation: For a finite set M, $|M|$ denotes its cardinality. It is the number of distinct elements and also the shortest possible length of a listing of M. The expression $|M|<\infty$ is sometimes used as shorthand for “M is finite”; infinite sets can have different cardinalities.
pitfalls: Repeated mentions of the same element do not increase the cardinality.
“Infinite” does not denote one single cardinality.
entries.heading: Endliche Mengen und Mächtigkeit

entries.short: The power set 𝒫(M) contains exactly all subsets of M.
entries.explanation: $A\in\mathcal{P}(M)\iff A\subseteq M$ holds; the elements of the power set are therefore themselves sets. For a finite set M with k elements, the power set has $2^k$ elements, since each element of M can independently be included in or excluded from a subset. The notation $2^M$ is also used for the power set.
entries.example: For M = {a, b}, 𝒫(M) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}, and thus |𝒫(M)| = 4.
pitfalls: The power set is a set of subsets, not merely another subset of M.
$\varnothing\subseteq M$ holds for every set M, but $\varnothing\in M$ does not necessarily hold.
entries.heading: Potenzmenge

entries.short: A bit string can encode a subset by indicating with each bit whether the corresponding element is included.
entries.explanation: Arrange the elements of a finite set M with k elements in a fixed order. For each element, write a 1 if it belongs to the subset A and a 0 if it does not. Thus, each subset corresponds to exactly one bit string of length k, and there are $2^k$ such strings.
entries.example: For M = {a, b, c} in the order a, b, c, `101` encodes the subset {a, c}.
pitfalls: The assignment of bit positions to elements depends on the specified order.
entries.heading: Bitfolgen als Merkhilfe

entries.short: Here, a family of sets is a nonempty set whose elements are themselves sets.
entries.explanation: A nonempty family of sets 𝒮 consists of sets as its members. One can form a union over the family and an intersection over the family. For a finite indexed family, the sets are often written as M₁, …, Mₖ.
entries.example: 𝒮 = {{1, 2}, {2, 3}} is a family of sets with two members.
pitfalls: The members of a family of sets are sets, not necessarily individual numbers or other basic elements.
entries.heading: Vereinigung und Schnitt ganzer Mengenfamilien

entries.short: The union over a family of sets contains the elements that belong to at least one member of the family.
entries.explanation: For a family of sets 𝒮, $\bigcup\mathcal{S}=\{x\mid\exists M\in\mathcal{S}:x\in M\}$ holds. For a finite indexed family, the corresponding notation is $\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}M_i$. This generalizes the union of two sets to any number of family members.
pitfalls: An element needs to belong to only one member of the family to be in the union over the family.
entries.heading: Vereinigung und Schnitt ganzer Mengenfamilien

entries.short: The intersection over a family of sets contains the elements that belong to every member of the family.
entries.explanation: For a nonempty family of sets 𝒮, $\bigcap\mathcal{S}=\{x\mid\forall M\in\mathcal{S}:x\in M\}$ holds. For a finite indexed family, the corresponding notation is $\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}M_i$. An element belongs to the intersection only if it occurs in every member of the family.
pitfalls: An element that belongs to only some members of the family is not in the intersection over the family.
An intersection over an empty family is not defined here; a universal set would have to be specified for that.
entries.heading: Vereinigung und Schnitt ganzer Mengenfamilien

entries.short: A partition divides a set into nonempty, pairwise disjoint blocks whose union is the entire set.
entries.explanation: A partition Π of M satisfies $\Pi\subseteq\mathcal{P}(M)$; each block $C\in\Pi$ is nonempty, distinct blocks are disjoint, and $\bigcup\Pi=M$. Thus, every element of M belongs to exactly one block. These conditions ensure that no element is omitted or assigned more than once, and that no block is empty.
entries.example: A partition of ℤ consists of the even and odd integers: {2ℤ, 1 + 2ℤ}.
pitfalls: Pairwise disjointness alone is not enough: the blocks must also cover the entire set.
Empty blocks are not allowed.
entries.heading: Partitionen

entries.short: In a Gray order, consecutive bit strings differ in exactly one bit.
entries.explanation: The cells of a KV diagram are arranged so that adjacent cells differ in only one membership bit. This places cases with nearly identical membership patterns next to each other. For several sets, the arrangement is distributed across rows and columns.
entries.example: The sequence `00`, `01`, `11`, `10` is a Gray order: each pair of consecutive bit strings differs in one bit.
pitfalls: The sequence of cells is not simply an ordinary ascending binary count.
entries.heading: Venn- und Karnaugh-Veitch-Diagramme
